name: Samjok-o
description: A three-legged crow that lives in the sun, central to East Asian solar mythology. In Korea, the Samjok-o was a Goguryeo-era emblem of imperial authority and the sun, attested on 6th–7th-century tomb murals; cognate figures are the Chinese Sanzuwu / Jinwu and the Japanese Yatagarasu.
full_description: The Samjok-o (삼족오, 三足烏) — literally 'three-legged crow' — is a solar bird shared across Chinese, Korean and Japanese mythology. The bird is said to live in the sun and to embody its power; in Chinese tradition, ten such crows once perched on the Fusang mulberry tree and took turns crossing the sky in Xihe's sun-chariot until the archer Hou Yi shot down all but one of them. In Korea, the Samjok-o is most strongly identified with the Goguryeo kingdom (37 BCE–668 CE), where it appears on multiple painted tomb murals of the 4th–7th centuries CE, often flanked by a dragon and a phoenix and explicitly representing the sun and the legitimacy of the Taewang ('Greatest of Kings'). Goguryeo and later Korean iconography treated the Samjok-o as superior in rank to both the dragon and the bonghwang (Korean phoenix). The Japanese Yatagarasu — described in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki as the divine crow that guided Emperor Jimmu from Kumano to Yamato — is a cognate figure, depicted with three legs in later art under Chinese influence and now used as the emblem of the Japan Football Association. The Samjok-o has been revived as a Korean cultural symbol since the 2000s, appearing in television dramas (notably 'Jumong' and 'The Legend'), corporate logos and national-identity discourse.

aliases.name: Jinwu
aliases.meaning: 'golden crow' — common variant name for the sun crow

aliases.name: Yatagarasu
aliases.meaning: 'eight-span crow' — Japanese counterpart, often three-legged in later art

regions: Goguryeo cultural sphere (Korean peninsula and southern Manchuria)
origin: East Asian: China (Sanzuwu / Jinwu), Korea (Samjok-o, especially Goguryeo), and Japan (Yatagarasu).

etymology.origin: East Asian solar bird mythology shared between China, Korea, and Japan
etymology.first_use: Bird-Sun motifs documented archaeologically in China from the Neolithic period; the three-legged form is established by the Han dynasty and dominant in Goguryeo tomb art by the 5th–6th century CE

timeline.event: Han-dynasty Mawangdui silk painting depicting a sun with a crow inside it (datable to c. 168 BCE)
timeline.significance: Among the earliest visual attestations of the sun-crow motif
timeline.source: Mawangdui tomb 1 silk banner, Hunan Provincial Museum

timeline.event: Samjok-o appears on Goguryeo tomb murals (e.g. Ssang-yong-chong, Anak Tomb No. 3 cluster, Deokheung-ri, etc.) flanked by dragon and phoenix
timeline.significance: Establishes the Samjok-o as a Goguryeo imperial symbol; date approximate (5th–7th c.)
timeline.source: Goguryeo tomb mural inventory; UNESCO World Heritage documentation

timeline.event: Compilation of the Kojiki, recording Yatagarasu as the divine three-legged crow that guides Emperor Jimmu
timeline.significance: Foundational Japanese textual attestation of the cognate figure

timeline.event: MBC television drama 'Jumong' premieres, prominently using the Samjok-o as the Goguryeo state emblem
timeline.significance: Major modern revival of the Samjok-o in Korean popular culture

related.name: Sanzuwu / Jinwu
related.description: Chinese three-legged sun crow; the direct cognate from which the Korean and Japanese forms derive

related.name: Yatagarasu
related.description: Japanese three-legged crow, divine guide of Emperor Jimmu

related.name: Bonghwang
related.description: Korean phoenix; frequently paired with the Samjok-o on Goguryeo tomb murals

related.name: Fenghuang
related.description: Chinese phoenix, structurally complementary to the Sanzuwu

related.name: Qilin / Kirin
related.description: Another auspicious East Asian mythical creature in the same iconographic family

cultural_notes: The Samjok-o connotes solar power, divine authority, and dynastic legitimacy in Korean tradition.
